title: Null Values
description: Model missing information deliberately, distinguish NULL from empty and zero values, and compare optional SQL values with precise semantics.
notes:
## Missing information needs a meaning

SQL NULL is a marker for absence of an ordinary value. A student's email might be unknown because it has not been supplied. An assessment score might be missing because marking has not finished. In each case, the schema and application should define what the absence means. NULL does not explain its own cause, and a consumer should not invent a reason merely because a cell appears blank.

Different causes can matter to users. A missing supervisor identifier might mean the student has not yet been assigned a supervisor, while a missing optional accommodation detail might mean the field does not apply. SQL ordinarily represents both absences with the same NULL marker. If the distinction affects decisions, model an explicit reason or state rather than expecting NULL alone to encode several business meanings.

## NULL differs from familiar placeholder values

Zero is a known numeric value. An empty string is a known string value, and the text 'NULL' is a string containing four letters. These values are different from SQL NULL. A student with zero recorded marks has a different fact from a student whose marks are not recorded. Treating the two identically can distort eligibility decisions, averages, and follow-up actions.

Avoid using arbitrary sentinel values such as minus one unless the data contract deliberately reserves and explains them. A sentinel may accidentally enter calculations as an ordinary value. Likewise, replacing a missing email with an empty string discards the distinction between absence and an explicitly supplied empty string. The representation should preserve the distinctions the application actually needs instead of merely making a grid appear complete.

## Ordinary equality does not test absence

SQL comparisons can return TRUE, FALSE, or UNKNOWN. A standard equality comparison involving NULL yields UNKNOWN, including NULL = NULL. The inequality NULL <> NULL is also UNKNOWN, not TRUE. This is why reasoning that two NULLs are simply unequal is misleading. Missing information does not establish either ordinary equality or ordinary inequality through those operators.

WHERE keeps rows whose predicate is TRUE. UNKNOWN rows do not pass, so WHERE email = NULL does not select missing emails. Use email IS NULL for absence and email IS NOT NULL for presence. Those predicates make the intended population explicit. A correctly named report can still be empty for the wrong reason if its filter uses ordinary equality against NULL.

## Read predicates as statements about knowledge

A score greater than fifty is unknown when score is absent. Negating that comparison does not magically establish that the student has a score of fifty or less. UNKNOWN remains UNKNOWN under NOT. A report of missing scores therefore needs its own absence condition rather than relying on the complement of a passing-score condition to include everybody else.

Combining conditions also needs care. A known TRUE alternative can make an OR predicate true even when another alternative is unknown. A known FALSE requirement can make an AND predicate false. Test the intended combinations directly instead of replacing three-valued reasoning with assumptions borrowed from ordinary two-valued Boolean expressions. The result should follow the specified student population, not a convenient interpretation of a blank cell.

## Optionality is separate from the value range

A score domain may permit integers from zero through one hundred, while a separate nullability policy permits absence until marking finishes. NOT NULL makes an ordinary value mandatory. A primary key forbids NULL because each key component must supply a definite identifying value. A nullable descriptive attribute follows a different rule because it need not identify the tuple.

An enforced CHECK condition is also distinct from NOT NULL. In MySQL 8.4, CHECK accepts an unknown condition as well as a true one. A score-range check can therefore permit an absent score unless nullability forbids it. State both policies when designing required scores: which recorded values are allowed and whether missing information is allowed at all.

## Duplicate handling has defined SQL rules

Ordinary equality is not the only operation that compares information in SQL. DISTINCT and GROUP BY have specified handling for NULLs: repeated NULLs in a selected value can form one distinct output value or one group. It is incorrect to conclude that duplicate elimination becomes undefined simply because NULL = NULL is unknown in a WHERE predicate.

A nullable UNIQUE column in MySQL can allow multiple NULLs while rejecting repeated ordinary non-NULL values according to its comparison rules. This is an engine-specific constraint behaviour, not proof that NULL <> NULL is true. Other products and constraint options can differ, so avoid presenting a vague majority-of-databases claim as a portable rule. Specify the actual database and intended uniqueness contract.

## Aggregates can hide missing observations

COUNT(*) includes every qualifying row. COUNT(score) counts non-NULL score values. SUM and AVG ordinarily operate on non-NULL inputs, and an ungrouped SUM or AVG with no non-NULL inputs returns NULL. These behaviours can change the interpretation of a class report: an average of recorded scores does not describe a class-wide average that treats every unrecorded score as zero.

If a report needs both completeness and performance information, return a row count and a recorded-score count alongside the average. This shows how much data supports the statistic. A high average from two recorded scores should not be mistaken for complete evidence about a class of thirty students. Defaults used for presentation should not conceal missing observations from the underlying calculation.

## Defaulting is a business decision

COALESCE returns the first non-NULL expression in its argument list. It can supply a display label such as 'not supplied' for a missing contact address. It does not replace an empty string unless the expression explicitly handles that case too. Keeping this distinction visible helps avoid surprising users who intentionally supplied an empty value under the application's accepted contract.

A display fallback does not update the source column. It also should not be mistaken for the student's actual address or score. When numerical defaults are needed, explain why that replacement preserves the intended quantity. Using zero because it avoids a blank chart is insufficient if zero and unrecorded data imply different facts or actions.

## Comparing optional values deliberately

A change detector often needs to treat two absent optional values as unchanged and a transition between absent and present as changed. Ordinary inequality cannot implement that contract by itself because it produces UNKNOWN when either operand is NULL. MySQL provides the NULL-safe equality operator <=> for this purpose. It returns true for two NULL operands and false when exactly one operand is NULL.

```sql
SELECT student_id
FROM contact_changes
WHERE NOT (old_email <=> new_email)
ORDER BY student_id;
```

This query identifies changed optional email values under the column's applicable comparison rules. It does not imply byte-for-byte comparison under every collation. If exact case or byte distinctions matter, the schema and comparison policy need to specify them. A robust test fixture should include unchanged ordinary values, both values missing, and transitions in both directions.

## Joins can introduce missing output values

A preserving join can return NULL child attributes when a parent has no matching child. That absence in the result is not necessarily a stored NULL in an existing child record. To distinguish those situations, inspect a child identity that is guaranteed non-NULL for matched rows. An optional child description can itself be NULL and therefore is a poor test of whether a match exists.

This distinction matters for counts and diagnostics. A student with no assessment record differs from a student with an assessment record whose score is unrecorded. The query and report should preserve whichever distinction the task needs. Modeling both as one unexplained blank can lead to the wrong follow-up action even when the SQL runs successfully.

## Verify absence as an ordinary case

Test NULL, an empty string, the literal text NULL, a recorded zero where relevant, and unchanged optional values. Include rows that should not match as well as rows that should. Keep identifiers in diagnostic results so repeated names remain separate student facts. These small cases provide clearer evidence than a large fixture containing only complete ordinary values.

NULL handling becomes reliable when the missing-information policy is explicit. Separate absence from placeholders, use the correct predicates, interpret aggregates carefully, and choose comparison semantics that match the task. Then record the database engine used for verification instead of assuming one product's optional-value behaviour establishes every provider's behaviour.

questions.question_text: What does SQL NULL represent in a nullable student attribute?
options: The number zero
An absence marker whose business meaning must be defined, distinct from zero and the empty string
An empty string
The average of all other values in that column
questions.explanation: SQL NULL marks missing information, and the application must define what absence means for the attribute.

questions.question_text: How does SQL NULL differ from an ordinary score-domain value?
options: Yes, every domain implicitly includes NULL
It marks absence rather than an ordinary score; nullability is a separate policy
Only for numeric domains
Only if explicitly declared NOT NULL
questions.explanation: SQL NULL marks missing information, and the application must define what absence means for the attribute.

questions.question_text: What does the expression WHERE gpa = NULL evaluate to in SQL, regardless of actual data?
options: TRUE for rows where gpa is NULL
UNKNOWN, so it never matches any row (IS NULL must be used instead)
FALSE always
A syntax error that halts the query
questions.explanation: Comparisons with NULL yield UNKNOWN under three-valued logic, so '= NULL' never returns rows; 'IS NULL' is the correct construct.

questions.question_text: Why must SQL NULL comparisons and duplicate handling be explained using the rules of each operation?
options: It doesn't; NULL has no effect on set semantics
Ordinary NULL equality is UNKNOWN, while DISTINCT and grouping still have explicitly defined NULL handling
Because NULL always forces two tuples to be treated as identical
Because NULL increases cardinality automatically
questions.explanation: SQL duplicate elimination is not undefined: ordinary equality predicates and DISTINCT or GROUP BY have different specified semantics.

questions.question_text: Why can a primary key attribute never be NULL (entity integrity)?
options: Because NULL takes up more storage space
Because a key must uniquely and reliably identify every tuple, and NULL's ambiguous equality would undermine that guarantee
Because SQL syntax forbids it for performance reasons only
Primary keys actually CAN be NULL in the relational model
questions.explanation: Primary-key constraints require unique, non-NULL identifying values for every component; optional attributes have a separate absence policy.

questions.question_text: How do aggregate functions like SUM and AVG typically treat NULL values in a column?
options: They treat NULL as zero
They skip/ignore NULLs entirely when computing the aggregate
They cause the query to fail
They convert NULL to the column's maximum value
questions.explanation: Standard SQL aggregate functions ignore NULLs, which can affect results like AVG in ways that surprise users expecting NULL to count as 0.

questions.question_text: In MySQL, can a nullable UNIQUE column permit multiple NULLs?
options: No, UNIQUE forbids any NULLs at all
Yes; MySQL permits multiple NULLs in a nullable UNIQUE column while constraining non-NULL values
No, only exactly one NULL is ever allowed
Yes, but only if the column is also the primary key
questions.explanation: This is MySQL uniqueness behaviour. Neither NULL = NULL nor NULL <> NULL evaluates to TRUE through ordinary comparison.

questions.question_text: Which of these best distinguishes 'missing but applicable' from 'missing and inapplicable' NULLs?
options: SQL stores them using two different NULL markers

Conceptually, one means the value exists in reality but isn't recorded yet, while the other means the attribute doesn't apply at all to this tuple — though most DBMSs store both identically as one NULL marker
Missing but applicable NULLs are never allowed in primary keys, while inapplicable NULLs are
There is no conceptual difference between the two
questions.explanation: The two are a useful conceptual distinction, but nearly all real DBMSs represent both cases with the same single NULL marker internally.

questions.question_text: Which predicate selects students with no supplied email?
options: email = NULL
email IS NULL
email = 0
email = the string NULL
questions.explanation: IS NULL tests the absence marker.

questions.question_text: What is NULL <> NULL under ordinary SQL comparison?
options: TRUE
FALSE by ordinary inequality
UNKNOWN
A guaranteed syntax error
questions.explanation: Absence does not establish ordinary inequality.

questions.question_text: Does an empty email string automatically count as SQL NULL?
options: Yes; they are identical in MySQL
Only when sorted
No; it is a separate string value
Only when selected with an alias
questions.explanation: An empty string and an absence marker differ.

questions.question_text: How does MySQL NULL-safe equality compare two NULLs?
options: It returns UNKNOWN
It returns the string NULL
It always raises an error
It returns true
questions.explanation: The <=> operator implements the explicitly null-safe comparison.

questions.question_text: What does NOT(old_email <=> new_email) select?
options: Changes including transitions between absent and present
Only two missing values
Only unchanged values
Every row always
questions.explanation: Negating NULL-safe equality detects those optional-value changes.

questions.question_text: What does COALESCE(email, fallback) do to an empty string email?
options: It always returns fallback
It retains the empty string
It updates the source row
It creates a NULL
questions.explanation: COALESCE replaces NULL, not every blank-looking value.

questions.question_text: What can COUNT(score) conceal if interpreted as class size?
options: Every score equal to zero
The number of columns
Students whose score is missing
Every passing student
questions.explanation: COUNT(expression) excludes NULL values.

questions.question_text: What does an ungrouped AVG return when it has no non-NULL inputs?
options: Always zero
Always one hundred
An empty schema
NULL
questions.explanation: There are no recorded values from which to compute an average.

questions.question_text: Does DISTINCT over a nullable selected value have undefined duplicate handling?
options: No; SQL defines its treatment of NULLs
Yes; it can never run
Only if NULL equals zero
It requires a primary key on every result
questions.explanation: Ordinary equality semantics do not make DISTINCT undefined.

questions.question_text: What distinguishes a missing child record from a child with an optional NULL description?
options: Test only the description
Test a guaranteed non-NULL child identity after the preserving join
Compare the description = NULL
Count displayed blank cells
questions.explanation: The identity indicates whether a child actually matched.

questions.question_text: If missing and inapplicable need different actions, what is useful?
options: Assuming SQL has two automatic NULL markers
Replacing both with zero
An explicit documented reason or state
Relying on column order
questions.explanation: One NULL marker does not encode multiple reasons automatically.

questions.question_text: Does a display fallback update stored missing data?
options: Yes; COALESCE runs UPDATE
Only on empty tables
Only for numeric types
No; an ordinary SELECT computes an output value
questions.explanation: Presentation expressions are distinct from writes.

coding_problems.title: Find absent contacts without confusing placeholders
coding_problems.task: Return student_id for students whose email is SQL NULL. Do not include an empty string or the literal text NULL.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE students (student_id INT PRIMARY KEY, email VARCHAR(80) NULL);
constraints: Email strings are data; no emails are sent.
edge_cases: Empty and literal NULL strings are distinct from absence.
Every row or no row can have an absent email.
hints: Ordinary equality against NULL does not select missing contacts.
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT student_id FROM students WHERE email IS NULL ORDER BY student_id;
coding_problems.explanation: IS NULL selects the absence marker without interpreting ordinary strings as missing.

coding_problems.title: Detect optional contact changes with NULL-safe equality
coding_problems.task: Return student_id where old_email and new_email differ under MySQL NULL-safe equality. Both missing means unchanged; a change between NULL and empty string counts as changed. Use NOT with <=>. Comparisons follow the defined column collation; fixtures do not rely on case differences.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE contact_changes (student_id INT PRIMARY KEY, old_email VARCHAR(80) NULL, new_email VARCHAR(80) NULL);
constraints: No case-only differences occur in supplied fixtures.
The comparison syntax targets MySQL 8.4; local MariaDB checks are compatibility evidence.
edge_cases: Absence-to-present and present-to-absence both count as changes.
hints: Negate the result of NULL-safe equality.
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT student_id FROM contact_changes WHERE NOT (old_email <=> new_email) ORDER BY student_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The operator yields a definite comparison for NULL pairs, so negation preserves all specified transitions.

original_questions.question_text: What does a NULL value represent in a relation?
options: The number zero
A missing, unknown, or inapplicable value — not a member of any domain
An empty string
The average of all other values in that column
original_questions.explanation: NULL is a special marker for absent/unknown data, distinct from any real domain value including 0 or an empty string.

original_questions.question_text: Is NULL considered a value drawn from an attribute's domain?
options: Yes, every domain implicitly includes NULL
No, NULL is not a member of any domain — it marks the absence of a value
Only for numeric domains
Only if explicitly declared NOT NULL
original_questions.explanation: NULL sits outside all domains; it denotes missing data rather than a legitimate domain value.

original_questions.question_text: What does the expression WHERE gpa = NULL evaluate to in SQL, regardless of actual data?
options: TRUE for rows where gpa is NULL
UNKNOWN, so it never matches any row (IS NULL must be used instead)
FALSE always
A syntax error that halts the query
original_questions.explanation: Comparisons with NULL yield UNKNOWN under three-valued logic, so '= NULL' never returns rows; 'IS NULL' is the correct construct.

original_questions.question_text: How does NULL complicate the classical definition of a relation as a 'set of tuples with no duplicates'?
options: It doesn't; NULL has no effect on set semantics
Because NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN rather than TRUE, equality between tuples containing NULLs becomes ambiguous, undermining clean duplicate detection
Because NULL always forces two tuples to be treated as identical
Because NULL increases cardinality automatically
original_questions.explanation: Since NULL never compares as definitively equal to another NULL, the notion of 'duplicate tuple' (central to the set-based relation definition) becomes ambiguous.

original_questions.question_text: Why can a primary key attribute never be NULL (entity integrity)?
options: Because NULL takes up more storage space
Because a key must uniquely and reliably identify every tuple, and NULL's ambiguous equality would undermine that guarantee
Because SQL syntax forbids it for performance reasons only
Primary keys actually CAN be NULL in the relational model
original_questions.explanation: Entity integrity requires that primary keys always uniquely identify tuples; NULL's undecidable equality would break that guarantee.

original_questions.question_text: How do aggregate functions like SUM and AVG typically treat NULL values in a column?
options: They treat NULL as zero
They skip/ignore NULLs entirely when computing the aggregate
They cause the query to fail
They convert NULL to the column's maximum value
original_questions.explanation: Standard SQL aggregate functions ignore NULLs, which can affect results like AVG in ways that surprise users expecting NULL to count as 0.

original_questions.question_text: Does a UNIQUE constraint in most SQL databases typically allow more than one NULL in the same column?
options: No, UNIQUE forbids any NULLs at all
Yes, because NULL is not considered equal to another NULL for uniqueness checks, multiple NULLs are usually allowed
No, only exactly one NULL is ever allowed
Yes, but only if the column is also the primary key
original_questions.explanation: Since NULL <> NULL under three-valued logic, most DBMSs permit multiple NULLs in a UNIQUE column — a practical departure from pure set semantics.

Missing but applicable NULLs are never allowed in primary keys, while inapplicable NULLs are
There is no conceptual difference between the two
original_questions.explanation: The two are a useful conceptual distinction, but nearly all real DBMSs represent both cases with the same single NULL marker internally.
